phases.name: Frame the exact brief and workload unknowns
phases.description: Carry the supplied problem record forward unchanged and identify workload details that must be learned before sizing or promising freshness.

phases.name: Ingest and land source data
phases.description: Use Data Factory to orchestrate source ingestion into Data Lake Storage Gen2 while keeping source cadence, schema, and retention decisions explicit.

phases.name: Transform and serve analytical queries
phases.description: Connect the lake to Synapse with the hinted PolyBase path, then validate transformations, query behavior, concurrency, and compute choices against the supplied constraints.

phases.name: Deliver governed business intelligence
phases.description: Expose approved analytical data to Power BI and make ownership, classification, lineage, and access controls part of the design.

phases.name: Validate scale, cost, and acceptance evidence
phases.description: Define safe behavior for incomplete or failed loads and require workload evidence before claiming any stated target is met.

steps.phase: Frame the exact brief and workload unknowns
steps.title: Start from the supplied problem record
steps.content:
Problem brief copied verbatim from the frozen problem fixture:
Title: Design an Enterprise Data Warehouse Solution
Description: Design a data warehouse solution that ingests data from multiple sources, transforms and cleanses data, runs complex analytical queries, and creates interactive dashboards.
Requirements:
- Ingest data from multiple sources
- Transform and cleanse data
- Store structured and semi-structured data
- Run complex analytical queries
- Create interactive dashboards
- Implement data governance
- Schedule ETL pipelines
- Support business intelligence
Constraints:
- Query performance under 5 seconds
- Support concurrent users (500+)
- Handle petabyte-scale data
- Minimize ETL processing time
- Cost-effective storage and compute
Hints:
- Synapse Analytics for warehousing
- Data Lake Storage Gen2 for storage
- Data Factory for ETL orchestration
- Power BI for visualization
- PolyBase for data integration
- Dedicated SQL pools for performance

Treat those requirements, constraints, and hints as the scope. No ingestion cadence, freshness promise, source inventory, workload mix, pool size, or budget is supplied, so keep those as questions rather than assumptions.

steps.phase: Frame the exact brief and workload unknowns
steps.title: Collect the workload facts before sizing
steps.content: Ask which source systems and owners are in scope, what formats and change signals they expose, how often data must arrive, which queries and dashboards matter, and what freshness users expect. Clarify the data classification, governance owner, recovery expectations, and compute budget before selecting detailed policies or capacity.

decision.question: Which missing inputs block a defensible warehouse design?
decision.chosen: Keep source inventory, data shape, ingestion cadence, query mix, freshness, governance policy, recovery expectations, and budget open until the owners provide them.
decision.chosenReason: The brief gives scale and query constraints but not the workload shape or operating policy needed to choose formats, refresh behavior, or capacity.

alternatives.option: Assume batch cadence and a fixed freshness window
alternatives.tradeoff: It would turn an unstated operating expectation into a requirement and could make the dashboards stale or unnecessarily expensive.

alternatives.option: Size services from the petabyte-scale statement alone
alternatives.tradeoff: Stored volume does not describe ingest rate, query concurrency, data distribution, or compute demand.

steps.phase: Frame the exact brief and workload unknowns
steps.title: Represent the source boundary without inventing systems
steps.content: Keep the source inventory as an explicit placeholder until the owning teams identify the systems, access methods, and data contracts.

component.label: Source Systems (inventory TBD)
component.description: Placeholder for the source systems named by their owners, with formats, access methods, data contracts, and change signals confirmed during discovery.

properties.purpose: Represent only confirmed source systems and their data contracts; no vendor, format, cadence, or change feed is assumed.

component.highlightReason: The brief requires multiple sources but does not name them, so the architecture keeps their details unresolved.

steps.phase: Frame the exact brief and workload unknowns
steps.title: Add Data Factory as the orchestration boundary
steps.content: Use the hinted Azure Data Factory role to schedule and coordinate ingestion and transformation work. Connector choice and pipeline behavior remain subject to each confirmed source contract.

component.label: Azure Data Factory
component.description: Orchestrates scheduled ingestion and transformation pipelines while source-specific connectors, cadence, and recovery behavior are confirmed.

properties.purpose: Schedule and orchestrate source ingestion and ETL work; configure source-specific behavior only after its contract is known.

component.highlightReason: Data Factory is explicitly named as the ETL orchestration hint and supports the scheduling requirement.

steps.phase: Frame the exact brief and workload unknowns
steps.title: Connect confirmed sources to the ingestion pipeline
steps.content: The edge represents source extraction coordinated by Data Factory; the source protocol and schedule are selected per confirmed source.

connection.label: Schedule and coordinate source extraction
connection.description: Data Factory invokes the source-specific ingestion path after source ownership, access, and change behavior are confirmed.

steps.phase: Frame the exact brief and workload unknowns
steps.title: Choose schedules from source and freshness contracts
steps.content: A schedule is not specified by the brief. Set it only after each source owner confirms availability, change detection, permitted extraction load, and the business freshness expectation.

decision.question: How should the ETL schedule be chosen?
decision.chosen: Use a source-specific schedule that satisfies the confirmed freshness need and source limits, then make dependencies and late arrivals visible to operators.
decision.chosenReason: A single assumed cadence could overload a source or deliver data later than business users expect.

alternatives.option: Use the same fixed schedule for every source
alternatives.tradeoff: Sources can have different change patterns, access limits, and downstream dependencies.

alternatives.option: Run every pipeline as frequently as possible
alternatives.tradeoff: It can waste compute and create load without satisfying a confirmed business need.

steps.phase: Frame the exact brief and workload unknowns
steps.title: Keep source-specific extraction behavior explicit
steps.content: Confirm whether a source supports snapshots, change tracking, or another safe continuation point. Do not claim incremental ingestion or lossless replay until the source contract and pipeline behavior have been verified.

decision.question: What extraction behavior should each pipeline use?
decision.chosen: Select snapshot or incremental behavior per source based on its documented capabilities and the agreed recovery process.
decision.chosenReason: The source inventory and change signals are not present in the brief, so a universal extraction mode would be invented.

alternatives.option: Assume every source supports change capture
alternatives.tradeoff: Some sources may expose only snapshots or may not provide a reliable change cursor.

alternatives.option: Reload every source in full for every run
alternatives.tradeoff: Repeated full extraction may increase ETL time, source load, storage, and compute cost.

steps.title: Add Data Lake Storage Gen2 for source data
steps.content: Use the hinted lake storage boundary for structured and semi-structured inputs. Choose organization, access, and lifecycle behavior after the source formats and retention policy are known.

component.label: Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2
component.description: Lake storage for structured and semi-structured source data, with layout, access, and lifecycle settings based on confirmed workload and governance policy.

properties.purpose: Land source data for downstream transformation and analytics while keeping layout and lifecycle choices tied to confirmed access and retention needs.

component.highlightReason: Data Lake Storage Gen2 is explicitly named for storage and addresses structured and semi-structured data.

steps.title: Land source data through Data Factory
steps.content: Data Factory writes the confirmed source payloads to the lake using a layout that preserves the information needed for cleansing, replay, and later analytical use.

connection.label: Land structured and semi-structured data
connection.description: Pipeline output is written to the lake; the exact representation and retention are chosen from source contracts and governance policy.

steps.title: Separate landed data from approved analytical data
steps.content: Keep the original landed representation available for controlled reprocessing where policy permits, and publish transformed data only after quality checks pass. Do not assume a retention period or create extra copies without a recovery, audit, or query need.

decision.question: How should source data and transformed data be separated?
decision.chosen: Preserve a governed landing boundary and promote validated results into the analytical model, with retention and deletion rules owned by data governance.
decision.chosenReason: This keeps transformation and replay understandable while avoiding an invented retention promise or unnecessary duplicate storage.

alternatives.option: Overwrite landed data with each transformation
alternatives.tradeoff: It can remove the input needed to explain or safely repeat a transformation.

alternatives.option: Keep every copy indefinitely
alternatives.tradeoff: It may conflict with governance policy and make storage cost ineffective.

steps.title: Handle schema changes without hiding them
steps.content: Validate incoming fields and types against the source contract. Route incompatible changes for review, record which source shape produced each published dataset, and update transformations deliberately rather than silently dropping unfamiliar fields.

decision.question: What should happen when a source schema changes?
decision.chosen: Version and validate the transformation contract, then publish only a shape that downstream queries and governance owners have approved.
decision.chosenReason: Structured and semi-structured inputs need explicit handling when their shape evolves; silent coercion can corrupt analytics.

alternatives.option: Accept every new field automatically
alternatives.tradeoff: Unexpected fields or type changes can alter downstream meaning and access controls.

alternatives.option: Discard fields outside the current model
alternatives.tradeoff: Useful source information can be lost before its analytical value is reviewed.

steps.title: Watch storage growth and access before changing tiers
steps.content: Petabyte-scale data is a supplied constraint, but no growth curve, retention period, or access distribution is specified.

scaleTrigger.metric: Observed stored-data growth, retrieval patterns, and storage cost
scaleTrigger.action: Validate lake layout and lifecycle tiers against measured access and the approved retention policy before changing storage behavior.
scaleTrigger.impact: Keeps large-scale storage cost-effective without inventing a retention period or moving data that users still need.

steps.title: Avoid moving data into the warehouse without a query need
steps.content: Select the curated data needed by analytical queries and business intelligence. Keep less-used source detail in the governed lake when direct warehouse duplication has no measured benefit.

decision.question: Which landed data should be materialized for analytics?
decision.chosen: Promote data based on confirmed query, governance, and freshness needs, and retain other governed data in the lake until a use case justifies more compute or copies.
decision.chosenReason: Separating storage and compute choices helps control cost at the stated data scale.

alternatives.option: Copy every source object into the warehouse
alternatives.tradeoff: It can increase load and storage cost without improving the required query paths.

alternatives.option: Expose all lake objects directly to every dashboard
alternatives.tradeoff: It can bypass curated semantics, quality checks, and access review.

steps.title: Keep transformations close to the best-supported execution path
steps.content: Use Data Factory to coordinate pipeline dependencies. Place each transformation where the confirmed source and data shape can be processed efficiently, and benchmark whether work belongs in the pipeline or the warehouse before committing to a pattern.

decision.question: Where should cleansing and transformation execute?
decision.chosen: Choose the execution location per transformation using measured processing time, source constraints, query reuse, and compute cost.
decision.chosenReason: The brief asks to minimize ETL processing time but does not provide data shape or a workload that justifies a single execution location.

alternatives.option: Perform every transformation before landing
alternatives.tradeoff: It can make source replay and access to original records harder.

alternatives.option: Perform every transformation in the warehouse
alternatives.tradeoff: It can consume analytical compute for work that may be better handled elsewhere.

steps.title: Measure pipeline time by source and transformation
steps.content: Record duration and completion state for source extraction, cleansing, and publication so a slow stage can be isolated.

scaleTrigger.metric: Observed duration and failure rate for each pipeline stage
scaleTrigger.action: Tune the measured bottleneck, parallelizing independent work only when source limits and downstream capacity allow it.
scaleTrigger.impact: Reduces ETL processing time without creating unsupported source load or unnecessary compute spend.

steps.title: Make landing readiness visible to downstream work
steps.content: Record whether an expected source load completed, was delayed, or failed. Downstream transformations should consume a declared ready state rather than treating partial arrival as a complete dataset.

steps.title: Add Synapse with dedicated SQL pools as the warehouse
steps.content: Represent the hinted Synapse Analytics warehouse and dedicated SQL pool option. Pool configuration remains open until query shape, concurrency, and budget are known.

component.label: Azure Synapse Analytics (Dedicated SQL pools)
component.description: Analytical warehouse for cleansed data and complex queries, with dedicated SQL pool configuration selected from measured workload and cost evidence.

properties.purpose: Serve curated analytical data and complex queries; determine pool configuration from the confirmed workload and performance evidence.

component.highlightReason: Synapse Analytics and dedicated SQL pools are explicit hints for warehousing and query performance.

steps.title: Connect lake data to Synapse through the PolyBase path
steps.content: Use the hinted PolyBase integration path between lake data and Synapse, then validate that the actual formats and access pattern are supported in the target environment.

connection.label: Integrate lake data through PolyBase
connection.description: The warehouse reads or loads the governed lake data through a verified PolyBase path suited to the confirmed data shapes and queries.

steps.title: Let Data Factory coordinate warehouse transformations
steps.content: Data Factory coordinates the approved transformation and publication steps; the warehouse remains the analytical execution boundary where measurement supports it.

connection.label: Coordinate transformation and publication
connection.description: Data Factory starts and tracks warehouse work after the required lake inputs are ready, then exposes completion state to downstream consumers.

steps.title: Verify the PolyBase integration against real source shapes
steps.content: Before relying on PolyBase, verify support for the confirmed formats, access controls, and query patterns in the deployed configuration. Where it does not fit, choose a tested staged-load path and keep the reason explicit.

decision.question: When should the lake-to-warehouse path use PolyBase?
decision.chosen: Use PolyBase only for the confirmed lake data and workload that the target configuration supports; use a validated alternative load path for unsupported cases.
decision.chosenReason: The hint identifies PolyBase as an integration option, while the brief does not specify formats or query behavior that prove universal fit.

alternatives.option: Assume every source format and query works through PolyBase
alternatives.tradeoff: An unverified access path can fail or perform poorly after data and query behavior are known.

alternatives.option: Copy every lake record into the warehouse first
alternatives.tradeoff: It may add processing and storage cost without improving every analytical query.

steps.title: Model only confirmed analytical meaning
steps.content: Ask business users to define the entities, measures, joins, and access patterns behind their complex queries. Build warehouse tables and transformations from those definitions rather than inventing a star schema or business domain.

decision.question: What should determine the warehouse data model?
decision.chosen: Model the entities and measures required by approved analytical queries, and preserve traceability to the governed source data.
decision.chosenReason: The brief requires analytical queries but does not name business entities, dimensions, measures, or query plans.

alternatives.option: Choose a standard dimensional model before learning the queries
alternatives.tradeoff: A conventional model can still miss the actual business grain or access patterns.

alternatives.option: Expose source records without a curated model
alternatives.tradeoff: Different reports can calculate the same business concept inconsistently.

steps.title: Select dedicated pool capacity from measured demand
steps.content: The brief names dedicated SQL pools but gives no pool size or query distribution. Benchmark representative complex queries and concurrent sessions, then compare candidate capacity and cost before selecting a configuration.

decision.question: How should dedicated SQL pool capacity be chosen?
decision.chosen: Select pool configuration using representative query plans, concurrency behavior, data distribution, and the approved compute budget.
decision.chosenReason: The supplied user and query constraints do not determine a safe pool size without workload evidence.

alternatives.option: Choose a large pool from the data scale alone
alternatives.tradeoff: Stored volume alone does not show query demand and can make compute cost ineffective.

alternatives.option: Choose the smallest available pool without a workload test
alternatives.tradeoff: It may fail the stated query and concurrency constraints.

steps.title: Tune against the stated query-performance limit
steps.content: Measure representative complex queries and dashboard interactions against the supplied target of under 5 seconds. Agree whether the target applies per query or to the end-to-end dashboard interaction, then record the workload and response-time evidence before claiming it passes.

scaleTrigger.metric: Elapsed time and resource use for representative queries and dashboard interactions, checked against the supplied target of under 5 seconds
scaleTrigger.action: Run the agreed query and dashboard workload; inspect query plans, data layout, joins, and pool capacity, then repeat the measurement after changing a demonstrated bottleneck.
scaleTrigger.impact: Provides evidence that the stated query constraint is met under the intended workload rather than relying on a component choice alone.

steps.title: Test concurrent sessions without assuming a peak shape
steps.content: Model the stated 500+ concurrent users with realistic dashboard and analytical behavior, refresh patterns, and an agreed arrival profile. Derive the resulting query and session load from that profile, then measure the user-facing dashboard path; the user count alone does not specify simultaneous database sessions.

scaleTrigger.metric: Dashboard response time, query queueing, and resource pressure under the agreed workload representing 500+ concurrent users
scaleTrigger.action: Tune pool capacity, query design, and workload isolation using the measured user, refresh, and query profile.
scaleTrigger.impact: Shows whether the stated concurrency and query constraints can hold together for the actual workload.

steps.title: Reduce the measured ETL bottleneck
steps.content: Use pipeline and warehouse execution evidence to locate expensive cleansing, movement, or repeated computation.

scaleTrigger.metric: Stage duration, transferred data, and compute use for each approved pipeline
scaleTrigger.action: Remove redundant work and parallelize independent stages only when source limits, ordering, and warehouse capacity permit it.
scaleTrigger.impact: Reduces ETL processing time while keeping data correctness and cost visible.

steps.title: Choose how semi-structured data enters analytics
steps.content: Keep semi-structured source records available under governance, and project only the fields and relationships needed by approved queries. Validate how schema variation affects the chosen PolyBase or staged-load path.

decision.question: How should semi-structured records be exposed to analytical queries?
decision.chosen: Preserve source meaning in the lake and publish a validated analytical representation for the query fields business users approve.
decision.chosenReason: The brief requires both structured and semi-structured data but does not define formats or the business fields to expose.

alternatives.option: Flatten every field into warehouse columns immediately
alternatives.tradeoff: It can create unstable schemas and unnecessary transformation work.

alternatives.option: Leave every report to interpret raw records
alternatives.tradeoff: It can produce inconsistent definitions and repeated query cost.

steps.title: Balance warehouse compute with query value
steps.content: Compare the cost of dedicated pool use, repeated transformations, and materialized data with the query benefit each provides. The brief does not specify a budget or operating window, so leave those choices for the owner and workload evidence.

decision.question: How should compute cost be controlled?
decision.chosen: Tie pool use and materialization to measured query demand, required freshness, and an approved cost envelope.
decision.chosenReason: This preserves the cost constraint without inventing a budget or assuming when users need the warehouse.

alternatives.option: Keep all analytical compute active at a fixed level
alternatives.tradeoff: It may spend beyond the workload's useful demand.

alternatives.option: Minimize compute without validating query outcomes
alternatives.tradeoff: It can undermine the stated query and concurrency constraints.

steps.title: Represent Power BI as the dashboard boundary
steps.content: Use the hinted Power BI role for interactive dashboards and business intelligence. Keep workspace, semantic model, and audience choices open until the owners confirm them.

component.label: Power BI Dashboards
component.description: Interactive dashboard and business intelligence boundary for approved warehouse data, with workspace and audience details confirmed by the business owners.

properties.purpose: Present governed analytical data through interactive dashboards and business intelligence reports.

component.highlightReason: Power BI is explicitly named for visualization and the brief requires interactive dashboards and business intelligence.

steps.title: Serve dashboards from curated warehouse data
steps.content: Power BI consumes the approved analytical model from Synapse, preserving a clear boundary between governed warehouse data and dashboard presentation.

connection.label: Serve governed analytical models
connection.description: Power BI queries or refreshes the approved Synapse model according to the confirmed freshness and access policy.

steps.title: Define shared dashboard measures with business owners
steps.content: Agree on the meaning of measures, filters, and relationships before publishing shared dashboards. Reuse approved definitions so reports do not independently reinterpret the same business data.

decision.question: What belongs in the Power BI semantic model?
decision.chosen: Publish only measures and relationships approved by the business owners and trace them to governed warehouse data.
decision.chosenReason: The brief names dashboards and business intelligence but does not supply a domain model or metric definitions.

alternatives.option: Define business measures separately in every dashboard
alternatives.tradeoff: Users can see inconsistent results for the same business concept.

alternatives.option: Publish every warehouse field to every audience
alternatives.tradeoff: It can expose data without a clear business meaning or access review.

steps.title: Choose dashboard freshness after users define it
steps.content: The brief does not say how quickly a source change must appear in a dashboard. Confirm the freshness need and select the refresh or query behavior that meets it without weakening the query-performance or cost constraints.

decision.question: Should dashboards use imported data or query the warehouse directly?
decision.chosen: Choose the Power BI access mode from the confirmed freshness, query, concurrency, and cost requirements, then validate the complete dashboard path.
decision.chosenReason: A freshness target and query mix are not supplied, so a fixed access mode would be an unsupported assumption.

alternatives.option: Assume every dashboard can use imported data
alternatives.tradeoff: The refresh behavior may not meet the business freshness expectation.

alternatives.option: Assume every dashboard should query the warehouse directly
alternatives.tradeoff: The live query path may add load or fail the stated performance constraint.

steps.title: Represent governance without inventing a vendor
steps.content: The requirement calls for data governance but does not name a catalog or policy product. Keep the control boundary generic until the organization confirms its governance tooling and ownership.

component.label: Data Governance Controls (tooling TBD)
component.description: Generic boundary for approved data ownership, classification, lineage, quality, and access policies, with implementation tooling selected by the organization.

properties.purpose: Coordinate approved governance policy and evidence across lake data, warehouse models, and business intelligence access.

component.highlightReason: Data governance is an explicit requirement, while the supplied hints do not identify a governance product.

steps.title: Apply governance to lake data
steps.content: Apply the organization-approved ownership, classification, lineage, and retention controls to the lake, with policy details supplied by its governance owners.

connection.label: Govern lake data and lifecycle
connection.description: Approved governance policy determines who can access landed data and how its classification, lineage, and lifecycle are recorded.

steps.title: Carry governance into warehouse models
steps.content: Keep warehouse access and published model definitions aligned with the approved governance policy and source lineage.

connection.label: Govern warehouse data and models
connection.description: Approved ownership, access, classification, and lineage rules apply to curated warehouse data and analytical models.

steps.title: Govern dashboard access and shared definitions
steps.content: Grant dashboard audiences access according to approved policy and keep published measures traceable to their governed source data.

connection.label: Govern dashboard access and definitions
connection.description: Business intelligence audiences and semantic definitions follow the organization's approved access and governance rules.

steps.title: Name owners for quality and policy exceptions
steps.content: Assign ownership for source contracts, data-quality failures, classification, lineage, and approval of published measures. Keep the specific policy rules open until the organization identifies its data classes and obligations.

decision.question: Who approves data quality and governance exceptions?
decision.chosen: Require named source and data owners to approve policy changes and the handling of invalid or newly classified records.
decision.chosenReason: A governance component alone does not define who is accountable for the data or its use.

alternatives.option: Let each pipeline owner make policy decisions independently
alternatives.tradeoff: Controls and definitions can diverge across sources and reports.

alternatives.option: Publish exceptions without an owner
alternatives.tradeoff: Invalid or sensitive data can remain unresolved and visible to consumers.

steps.title: Enforce least privilege at each data boundary
steps.content: Define access for source extraction, lake objects, warehouse data, and Power BI audiences separately. Confirm the applicable data classification and user groups before selecting detailed permissions.

decision.question: How should access be granted across the warehouse path?
decision.chosen: Grant only the source, pipeline, analyst, and dashboard access approved for each role, and validate denied as well as permitted paths.
decision.chosenReason: Governance must remain effective as data moves from its source to reports, and the brief does not provide an identity or classification model.

alternatives.option: Use one broad identity for all pipeline and dashboard access
alternatives.tradeoff: It obscures ownership and makes least-privilege review difficult.

alternatives.option: Apply access only at the dashboard layer
alternatives.tradeoff: It leaves lake and warehouse data paths outside the same governance review.

steps.phase: Validate scale, cost, and acceptance evidence
steps.title: Keep late or unavailable sources from appearing current
steps.content: If a source is delayed or unavailable, retain the last successfully published dataset and expose the incomplete load state. Do not label partial arrival as current; agree with business owners how dashboards should communicate staleness.

decision.question: What should consumers see when an expected source load is incomplete?
decision.chosen: Preserve the last complete published result, record the load status, and apply a business-approved stale-data indication.
decision.chosenReason: This avoids presenting partial data as complete while leaving freshness semantics with the data owners.

alternatives.option: Publish whatever records arrived
alternatives.tradeoff: Queries can return a plausible but incomplete result.

alternatives.option: Replace the last good result with an empty result
alternatives.tradeoff: A temporary source issue can remove otherwise usable business intelligence.

steps.phase: Validate scale, cost, and acceptance evidence
steps.title: Make failed transformations safe to investigate and repeat
steps.content: Track input readiness and publication status for each pipeline run. Make retries safe for the selected source and transformation behavior, and prevent an incomplete warehouse update from being exposed as a completed dataset.

decision.question: How should a partially failed ETL run be recovered?
decision.chosen: Resume or replay from a verified boundary, validate the resulting data, and publish only after the agreed completion checks pass.
decision.chosenReason: Explicit completion boundaries reduce duplicate work and prevent partial results from silently reaching dashboards.

alternatives.option: Restart all work without checking what already completed
alternatives.tradeoff: It can repeat expensive extraction and transformation or create duplicate records.

alternatives.option: Continue downstream work after any upstream error
alternatives.tradeoff: It can publish data without complete or validated inputs.

steps.phase: Validate scale, cost, and acceptance evidence
steps.title: Validate the design at the stated data scale
steps.content: Petabyte-scale data is an explicit constraint. Use representative data shape and distribution at the required scale before claiming that storage, ETL, or analytical queries meet their targets.

scaleTrigger.metric: Ingest completion, transformation duration, query behavior, concurrency, and storage and compute cost at the required data scale
scaleTrigger.action: Run an end-to-end workload representative of the confirmed sources and queries, then adjust layout and capacity from observed bottlenecks.
scaleTrigger.impact: Separates a diagram-level design from evidence that the stated scale and cost constraints can be met.

steps.phase: Validate scale, cost, and acceptance evidence
steps.title: Require evidence for each supplied constraint
steps.content: Acceptance should verify representative complex queries under 5 seconds; the agreed dashboard and analytical workload representing 500+ concurrent users; representative petabyte-scale data; ETL duration against an owner-approved pipeline objective; and cost-effective storage and compute measured against an approved budget. Also verify source replay, governance enforcement, and dashboard correctness. Keep every target unverified until repeatable end-to-end evidence exists.

decision.question: What is sufficient evidence to accept the warehouse design?
decision.chosen: Require repeatable end-to-end results tied to the supplied constraints and confirmed workload, with failures and unresolved assumptions recorded.
decision.chosenReason: Selecting Azure components does not demonstrate query performance, scale, cost, governance, or dashboard correctness.

alternatives.option: Accept the architecture diagram as proof
alternatives.tradeoff: A diagram does not show measured behavior or policy enforcement.

alternatives.option: Validate only a small happy-path sample
alternatives.tradeoff: It does not establish behavior for the required data scale or concurrent workload.

steps.phase: Validate scale, cost, and acceptance evidence
steps.title: Review the design and unresolved owner decisions
steps.content: The draft uses the hinted Data Factory, Data Lake Storage Gen2, Synapse Analytics with dedicated SQL pools, PolyBase integration, and Power BI within the existing generic component catalog. Confirm source contracts, freshness, query mix, governance policy, recovery behavior, and budget before sizing or claiming that any supplied constraint has passed. This walkthrough is a local review draft, not evidence of deployment or publication.
